object_types.name: Customer
object_types.definition: A person or entity who places orders; identified by a unique customer ID in the CRM system.

source_references.excerpt: A customer places an order.
Each customer has a unique customer ID in the CRM system.
In our CRM they're "customers" but the billing team calls them "clients."

object_types.name: CustomerId
object_types.definition: The unique identifier for a customer in the CRM system.

source_references.excerpt: Each customer has a unique customer ID in the CRM system.

object_types.name: CustomerName
object_types.definition: The name of a customer, tracked as a plain text field.

source_references.excerpt: Yes, every customer has a name. It's just a text field.

object_types.name: Order
object_types.definition: A purchase transaction placed by a customer, containing one or more products.

source_references.excerpt: Every order belongs to exactly one customer, and customers can place multiple orders over time.
Each order has an order number. That's the primary identifier.

object_types.name: OrderNumber
object_types.definition: The primary identifier for an order.

source_references.excerpt: Each order has an order number. That's the primary identifier.

object_types.name: OrderStatus
object_types.definition: The status of an order, restricted to a fixed set of values.

source_references.excerpt: Yes, an order has a status. The possible values are: pending, confirmed, shipped, and delivered.

object_types.name: Product
object_types.definition: An item that can appear in one or more orders; identified by a unique SKU code.

source_references.excerpt: An order contains one or more products.
By SKU -- a unique stock-keeping unit code.

object_types.name: Sku
object_types.definition: A unique stock-keeping unit code identifying a product.

source_references.excerpt: By SKU -- a unique stock-keeping unit code.

object_types.name: Quantity
object_types.definition: The number of units of a product specified on an order line.

source_references.excerpt: Each line in the order specifies a product and a quantity.

ambiguities.description: The billing team's 'client' concept requires the customer to have actually paid, which may represent a different lifecycle state than a CRM 'customer'. Is 'Client' truly a synonym for 'Customer', or should it be modeled as a subtype/state (e.g., a Customer who has paid) with its own semantics?

source_references.excerpt: For our purposes they're the same concept but the billing team has a slightly different definition -- they only consider someone a client once they've actually paid.

ambiguities.description: It's stated an order 'contains one or more products' via order lines with quantity, but no explicit uniqueness/cardinality was given for whether the same product can appear on multiple separate lines within the same order (composite uniqueness assumed per order-product pair). Confirm whether duplicate product lines within one order are allowed.

source_references.excerpt: Each line in the order specifies a product and a quantity.

ambiguities.description: No explicit statement addresses whether an Order's total amount or line totals are stored or derived from product price and quantity; product price itself was never discussed. Clarify if pricing/monetary data needs to be captured in the model.

source_references.excerpt: An order contains one or more products. Each line in the order specifies a product and a quantity.

ambiguities.description: It is unclear whether the Customer-Order relationship should track historical changes (e.g., can an order be reassigned to a different customer) or if this is strictly a current-state, immutable relationship.

source_references.excerpt: Every order belongs to exactly one customer, and customers can place multiple orders over time.

ambiguities.description: No frequency or upper bound was given for how many orders a customer can place, or how many products can appear on a single order line -- these are left unbounded by default, which should be confirmed with stakeholders.
